question.text: Deepak has not rebalanced his portfolio in 3 years despite significant equity appreciation. He avoids making changes because he fears that any action might lead to regret. His adviser notes that Deepak feels regret from commission (acting) more strongly than regret from omission (not acting). Richard Thaler's solution to this type of bias is:

answer.text: Providing detailed past performance data to build confidence
Reducing the number of investment options available to the client
Auto-enrollment or default options, such as automatic pension plan enrollment (nudging)
Increasing the client's exposure to financial literacy workshops

explanation.text: The Logic: Deepak's inaction reflects status quo bias linked to regret aversion — the workbook notes that regret from commission feels more intense than regret from omission. Richard Thaler's simple nudge, illustrated in the workbook with automatic enrollment in pension plans, addresses this by making the desired action the default so the bias toward inaction works in the investor's favour. The Trap: Financial literacy workshops target knowledge gaps rather than the regret-aversion mechanism described. Providing past performance data does not change the choice architecture, and reducing options speaks to choice paralysis, not the Thaler nudge for status quo bias. Note: When the prompt cites regret from commission versus omission and a Thaler-style fix, anchor to the workbook's auto-enrollment / default-option nudge.
